title: The Peace of Wild Things
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart's talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating stillness and presence in our daily lives, drawing inspiration from their own experiences with vertigo and nature. They encourage us to come into contact with wild things and find peace in the natural world, which can bring freedom from our thoughts and worries. Through practices like Zazen and meditation, we can develop mindfulness and clarity, allowing us to navigate life's challenges with greater ease and inner peace.

sentences.text: Good morning, dear friends.
Thank you for your patience with me.
I've been dealing with some vertigo for the last two weeks, and it's stressful, and you're never out trying to bother everyone away.
So, I'm better at mentioning.
Good morning and welcome to Zen Alive.
You may also be surprised to hear from me again so soon, but unfortunately, our speaker for the dharma talk cancelled with very short notice.
We are all so busy.
The days are so short.
There's stuff to do, so much to accomplish.
We are caught up with what is going on in the news, in our county, in our country, in courtrooms and boardrooms.
So, today, I want to remind us of wildness and wilderness, mountains and waters, and zazen.
As the opening, I am offering a poem by Wendell Berry, calling us to the peace of wild things and the presence of still water.

*When despair for the world grows in me, and I wake in the night at the least sound in fear of what my life and my children's lives may be, I go and lie down where the wood drake rests in his beauty on the water and the great heron feeds.
I come to the peace of wild things who do not tax their lives with forethought of grief.
I come to the presence of still water.
And I feel above me the day blind stars waiting with their light.
For a time, I rest in the grace of the world and then free.
I love this poem.
And last week, our Reading Dogen study group has started on the Mountains and Waters Sutra.
This sutra often brings up thoughts of nature and wildness and wilderness in my mind.*

In my essay Walking, Henry David Thoreau wrote, "I wish to speak a word for nature, for absolute freedom and wildness, as contrasted with a freedom and culture merely civil, to regard man as an inhabitant or a part and parcel of nature, rather than a member of society."
This makes me think that Thoreau knew something of zazen.
In the same essay, he also wrote, "in wildness is the preservation of the world."
In my heart, wildness and zen and love live closely together, intimately.
All these things that want to live without boundary, that want to live in boundlessness, in emptiness, free from all that thou shalt and thou shalt not.
Let's sit with that for a couple of minutes.
Let us close our eyes and look for it in ourselves, because I'm sure you have things like that in your heart, too.
I will ring a bell to start and end our short set.
I want to remember this place in my heart often.
It is precious.
Dogen also seems to touch on this place when he begins the Mountains and Waters Sutra.
These mountains and waters of the present are the expression of old Buddhas, each abiding in its own dharmic state, fulfills exhaustive virtues.
Because they are the circumstances prior to the kalpa of emptiness, they are this life of the present.
Because they are the self before the germination of any subtle sign, they are liberated in their actual occurrence.

Since the virtues of the mountains are high and broad, the spiritual power to ride the clouds is always mastered from the mountains, and the marvelous ability to follow the wild is inevitably liberated from the mountains.
End quote.
Do you understand this?
Are these circumstances this life of the present?
I don't know, and I do not really understand.
When I first encountered Dogen, I did want to know, and I did want to understand.
I once wanted to explain it to you.
I translated Dogenese into Mekong.
Mekong Crap.
And what did I do?
I safely packed it up and put it in the front door.
The virtues of the mountains are high and broad.
The spiritual power to ride the clouds is always mastered from the mountains, and the marvelous ability to follow the wild is inevitably liberated from the mountains.
About the mountains, while they put a button, I never figured it out.
Of course, Dogen is not only talking about mountains.
He is talking about our life, this whole world, and human society.
And how do we grasp it?
Well, I think, don't ask it, don't ask for it.
We get it, and we don't get it.
We are in the virtues of the mountains so high and broad.
Maybe during zazen, for the briefest moment, we mastered the spiritual power to ride the clouds.
Then we know that we are in the mountains.
And maybe one day, unexpectedly, we open the hand of thought and we liberate the marvelous ability to follow the wild.
The wild changes continuously according to place and season and circumstance, though we always know it when we experience it.
We, as practitioners of Zen, we practice zazen.
We actively and intentionally do what Wendell Berry touched on in his poem.
We go and lie down where the wood drake rests in his beauty on the water and the great heron feeds.
We come to the place of wild things who do not tax their lives with forethought of grief.
We come into the presence of still water and for a time we can rest in the grace of the world and we are free.
Our way is to sit every day and get in touch with ourself.
The self we get in touch with is not the conditioned one who usually runs the show.
I admit, sometimes this sitting is difficult for me.
Anxiety, fear, boredom, thoughts, emotions.
The monkey mind is a life and well, and it's a life in the time of zazen too.
One of my favorite Zen practices is the one I learned first, breath counting meditation.
Breath is a link between mind and body.
It is one of the few physiological processes that function both voluntarily and involuntarily.
To a certain extent we can consciously control it, and when we don't want to control it, it happens automatically.
We can slow down and speed up our breathing, but we cannot stop it altogether voluntarily.
Our emotions and external conditions are reflected in our breathing pattern.
When we get excited, we breathe faster.
When we are in a rush, we fight.
When we are calm, our breathing is deep and regular.
In zazen, we breathe naturally.
Without engaging in techniques such as square breathing, we do however count our exhalations from one to ten.
When I get distracted, back to one.
When I lose count, back to one.
I realize I counted past ten, back to one.
Wow, I reached ten, back to one.
We just watch.
We watch the breath carefully with as much attention as a burglar breaking into a house.
Breath counting meditation is a strength building exercise for the mind, a calming exercise.
Little by little distracting thoughts come down.
The monkey mind may even take a break, and our concentration strengthens.
And yes, I may sit down for a period of zazen with a troubled mind and not get past three for the whole half hour.
Or I may get lost, and the first thing I notice is the bell that ends meditation.
And yet, the next time I sit down again, fully engaging, I am so grateful for this practice.
Shohaku Okumura wrote this about zazen: "Only in zazen, we stop making karma."
When we leave the zendo, we have to do something.
To do something, we have to make choices.
And the choices I make depend on my values, which are influenced by my karmic consciousness.
I cannot be free of karma even when I try to do things simply for the sake of dharma.
That is still my choice, and whenever I make a choice, I am making new karma, whether good or bad karma.
When we stand up from the cushion and go outside, we cannot let go of everything.
It would be dangerous.
When we leave the zendo, we have to think again.
Come to think of it, my sitting time is a small price to pay for the life I have, to not be so caught up by causes and conditions, the waves of externality not crashing into the shores nonstop.
Seeing things clearly, I come into the peace of wild things, and I come into the presence of still water.

Since the virtues of the mountain are high and broad, the spiritual power to ride the clouds is always mastered from the mountains, and the marvelous ability to follow the wild is inevitably liberated from the mountains.
Thank you, zazen, for the piece.
I would like to end today's talk with the Wendell Berry poem, Do Not Be Ashamed.
*You will be walking some night in the comfortable dark of your yard, and suddenly a great light will shine around about you and behind you will be a wall you never saw before.
It will be clear to you suddenly that you were about to escape and that you are guilty.
You misread the complex instructions, you are not a member, you lost your card or never had one.
And you will know that they have been there all along, their eyes on your letters and books, their hands in your pockets, their ears wired to your bed.
Though you have done nothing shameful, they will want you to be ashamed.
They will want you to kneel and weep and say you should have been like them.
And once you say you are ashamed, reading the page they hold out to you, then such light as you have made in your history will leave you.
They will no longer need to pursue you.
You will pursue them begging for forgiveness.
They will not forgive you.*
There is no power against them.
It is only candor that is aloof from them, only an inward clarity unashamed that they cannot reach.
Be ready.
When their light has picked you out and their questions are asked, say to them, "I am not ashamed."
A sure horizon will come around you and the heron will begin his evening flight from the hilltop.
